Built with Staircase

Brew State

A new controller for the Sunbeam EM7000 espresso machine: two mains-voltage boards, a six-layer main board and a small heater board on the machine's wall, designed and checked end to end by AI under human direction.

The main board replaces the machine's original controller and drops into the same place. The heater wall board is new: it carries the two heater switches out to the steel wall, where their heat has somewhere to go. The person directing the work is not an electronics engineer: he set the goals and made the calls in discussion, and Staircase turned that into requirements, decisions and checks.

This page shows the two boards, and Staircase, the process that made them.

Two boards

One board does the thinking and sensing; the other only switches the heaters. Three wires join them.

  • Measures

    Thermistors, current sensors and pressure inputs on the controller's own converter. Two PT1000 probes in the water path. Two load cells, so a shot can end on measured weight. An isolated converter for mains voltage and total current. Flow-meter pulses and two digital pressure sensors.

  • Switches

    Two pumps through triacs, two valves through relays, and the heater triacs on a second board, each switch timed to the mains zero crossing.

  • Drops in

    Four mounting holes on the machine's four mounting points. Connectors sit where the machine's existing harnesses still reach: the mains tabs on the original edge in the original order, the low-voltage connectors moved within reach to suit the routing. The tank-level reed soldered through the back, where the float's magnet reaches it. The machine's own panel keys, knob switches, buzzer, flow meter and gauge steppers work as before, and the board has expansion for a touchscreen display.

Designed from models

The machine was modelled before the board was drawn: a plant model of the heaters, water and steam, and a state estimator for what cannot be measured. Which sensors the board carries is computed, not assumed. An identifiability analysis of the model shows, for each operating phase, what each sensor adds and how far the estimate error grows without it. It covers supply voltage and current, the water temperature leaving each heated block, and brew pressure beside flow, where neither alone reveals the resistance of the coffee puck.

The compiled firmware runs under emulation against a model of every channel the board provides, so the board and the code agree before anything is powered.

Safety first

The priorities, in order, on both boards: safety, never relaxed; then workmanship; then the performance rules that matter on this board; then cost.

  • Mains beside logic

    Every mains-to-logic gap holds at least 3.0 mm through air and 10.0 mm along the surface, and mains conductors stay 1.5 mm apart, as the signed separation record (IEC 60664-1) requires. Milled slots lengthen the surface path where parts bridge the barrier, one of them under the isolated converter.

  • Total power from one shunt

    Pumps and valves switch on the neutral side, so every return current, the heater's included, passes one shunt, read from across the barrier.

  • Power that cannot stick on

    The main relay closes only while the controller keeps sending a heartbeat. If the software stops, the relay opens.

  • Protection at both ends

    A 10 A fuse, varistor, X2 capacitor and inrush limiter guard the entry; three branch fuses guard the loads; TVS diodes clamp the pump triacs. Opto-triacs fire the triacs, so the controller only ever drives an LED.

  • Quiet measurement

    An unbroken ground layer lies under the logic, and every routing layer has a ground layer beside it.

Made to look right

Autorouted boards rarely look drawn by an engineer. The AI was tasked to make the main board as neat as it reasonably could. It did that by planning the routing before placing the parts.

Some things were fixed: the mounting holes, the mains zone and the reed, and every connector had to stay within its harness's reach. Around them, the controller's pins were assigned and the chip turned 180° so its pins face the way their routes run. Trial routes on scratch copies found the hotspots before any copper was kept; one led to ten small parts moving so two of the controller's pins could escape.

The copper was then drawn block by block, by script, to a written rulebook, and looked at. Rules judge legality and measurable workmanship; agents review pictures of every layer, blind, and each round fed the next. Mains copper has 45° mitred corners; ground pours have smooth arcs.

    Built to be made

    Assembly
    Parts come from the fabricator's own catalogue, and the fabricator assembles them, all on the top side.
    Rules
    Design rules taken from the fabricator's published limits for a six-layer board; the wall board uses the same fabricator's two-layer limits.
    Cost
    Standard options only: 1 oz outer copper, 0.3 mm drills, no impedance control.
    Stress
    Parts held to a written derating policy based on NASA's published derating table.

    Board two

    The heater wall board

    The two heaters draw about 5.4 A each, and the switches that run them get warm. So they sit on a small second board on the machine's steel wall, where the wall can carry their heat away, and the main board drives them over three low-voltage wires.

    Copper
    2 layers
    Size
    45 × 75 mm
    Parts
    15 footprints
    Current
    5.4 A per heater, 10.2 A on the shared return
    Mains copper
    5–6 mm strips, both layers
    Vias
    None on any mains net
    Mains to logic
    10.7 mm along the surface
    Link
    3 pins: 5 V and two LED returns
    • Switches

      Two identical chains, one per heater. An opto-triac (onsemi MOC3083, a light-coupled switch, so the main board only ever lights an LED) fires an insulated 16 A triac (ST BTA16-800BW, the mains switch itself) through two gate resistors. It fires only near the mains zero crossing, so the heater switches on without a spike. A varistor across each output clamps surges. The heaters switch on the neutral side, as the main board's loads do.

    • Cools

      The two triacs stand on the board's top edge with their tabs screwed to a flat aluminium plate, and the plate bolts to the steel wall. The triacs are the insulated kind, so the tab needs no separate insulating pad.

    • Fits

      Blade terminals for the element harness and the return sit on the edge away from the plate, so the mains wires come in from that side and do not cross the parts. A 3D-printed case will hold the board on the plate, with a wall in its tray between the mains copper and the earthed plate, and a lid that comes off with the board still in the machine.

    How it was proven

    • Calculated

      Records work out each part's stress, heat and spacing from its datasheet; the margin checks pass, 17 of 17.

    • Reviewed

      The schematic went through 14 rounds of review against those records. Each finding was closed by a change, or by the owner accepting it in his own words (10 written acceptances).

    • Planned, then drawn

      A layout plan weighed the board against a catalogue of 70 layout practices before any copper. Placement was picked from candidate layouts, the whole board was routed once as a trial, and then routed for real: every connection made, no via on a mains net, 10.7 mm from mains to logic. KiCad's own design-rule check is clean apart from closely spaced pad pairs the owner has accepted.

    How it was made: Staircase

    1. Discuss

      Work starts with a conversation about goals. Discussion is the only way the owner steers the project.

    2. Derive

      From that direction and its dependencies, Staircase works out the requirements, each with testable acceptance criteria, the decisions behind them, and a delivery roadmap.

    3. Keep

      A deterministic graph engine holds every requirement, decision, deliverable and piece of evidence, and the links between them, for the life of the project.

    4. Build and prove

      Staircase workflows let AI agents take the next piece of work, build it and check it. A requirement closes only when evidence meets each of its criteria.

    This project's graph: 73 requirements · 1,812 acceptance criteria · 68 decisions · 299 deliverables · 2,886 evidence records

    How it is checked

    Automated checks give the same answer every run, covering mains clearance and creepage, locked mains copper, connections, pad numbering, drills, fitted parts, workmanship rules and the fabricator's limits. The main board: 0 violations. The heater wall board goes through the same check before it is ordered; it has not yet. The checker is itself proven on faults planted in copies of a board, 380 of 380 caught, and its tools carry about 3,430 tests of their own.

    Brew State is open hardware, released into the public domain.
